documents: Tagawa, Helffrich, Hirose & Ohishi (2022), High-Pressure Melting Curve of FeH: Implications for Eutectic Melting Between Fe and Non-Magnetic FeH, JGR Solid Earth 127, e2022JB024365 (published PDF, 11 pages)

entry.evidence: phase relations in the Fe-FeH system remain largely unknown at high pressures and temperatures (P-T)

sequences.source_document: Tagawa et al. 2022, JGR Solid Earth, published PDF

steps.action: Posed the open question of the Fe-FeH phase diagram at core pressures, specifically the unknown melting curve of non-magnetic fcc FeH.
steps.quote: The melting curve of non-magnetic fcc FeH is not known.

steps.action: Took up Fukai's (1992) speculative Fe-H2 phase diagram, which assumes continuous Fe-FeH solid solution and was supported only below about 20 GPa.
steps.quote: assuming that Fe and FeH form a continuous solid solution

steps.action: Used their own earlier findings that stoichiometric FeH is fcc above about 50 GPa, unlike hcp Fe, and loses its local spin moment above about 40 GPa.
steps.quote: Tagawa et al. (2022) also demonstrated that FeH loses its local spin moment [...]

steps.action: Proposed a rival to continuous solid solution: the structural difference between Fe and FeH above about 50 GPa changes the Fe-FeH diagram.
steps.quote: the different crystal structure between Fe and FeH above ∼50 GPa will probably change the Fe-FeH phase diagram significantly

steps.action: Set laboratory conditions. They synthesized stoichiometric FeH from Fe + H2 in a laser-heated DAC with an NaCl inner gasket, then removed excess H2 at cryogenic temperature so the sample was H-undersaturated. They then reached 43-152 GPa and up to 4630 K, with spectroradiometric temperature, NaCl-based pressure and synchrotron XRD at BL10XU.
steps.quote: we opened the sample chamber to remove excess H2 without decomposition of FeH

steps.action: Built a thermodynamic model by extending low-pressure metallurgical (CALPHAD-type) models of Fe hydrides to high pressure. It combines Birch-Murnaghan pressure terms with a Hillert-Jarl magnetic term, and its pure-iron parameters were fitted to experimental phase boundaries and melting points.
steps.quote: Our thermodynamic model is based on low-pressure metallurgical models

steps.action: Checked sample stoichiometry. No FeH2 or FeH3 formed above 60 GPa, and 300 K unit-cell volumes before and after melting lay on the stoichiometric FeH compression curve.
steps.quote: which proved no excess hydrogen remained in the sample chamber

steps.action: In run #1, quenching from 2740 K produced additional hazy diffraction signals beside the fcc peaks, which were absent after quenching from 2480 K. They read these signals as crystals formed from quenched liquid.
steps.quote: additional “hazy” diffraction signals appeared close to the fcc peaks in the 2D and 1D XRD spectra

steps.action: Cross-checked the XRD melting criterion against a second method: an FIB cross-section of the run #1 sample, imaged by SEM, showed NaCl grains inside FeH metal, a melting texture.
steps.quote: in order to crosscheck the present melting criterion with a melting texture in a recovered sample

steps.action: Compared the quench products with what incongruent melting would yield. Only stoichiometric FeH crystallized from the liquid, so they concluded that FeH melts congruently.
steps.quote: We also noted that FeH melted congruently (liquid FeH coexisted with solid FeH)

steps.action: In runs #2-#5, applied the hazy-signal criterion to bracket melting between non-melting and melting conditions from 43 to 152 GPa, with runs #4-#5 targeted near the spin-loss pressure.
steps.quote: we explored the melting of stoichiometric FeH, by employing the appearance of the additional hazy diffraction signal

steps.action: Confirmed that melting caused no hydrogen heterogeneity: room-temperature FeH volumes always fell on a single P-V curve.
steps.quote: the unit-cell volumes of FeH collected at room temperature were always plotted in a single P-V curve

steps.action: Fitted the thermodynamic model to the melting and non-melting brackets plus Sakamaki et al.'s data below 20 GPa. The fitted melting curve steepens above about 40 GPa with the loss of magnetism.
steps.quote: The melting curve of FeH was obtained by fitting the thermodynamic model to these not-melting and melting data

steps.action: Compared the FeH melting curve with the published FeHx (1<x<2) eutectic temperatures. Non-magnetic FeH melts above them, whereas below 20 GPa the FeH solidus coincides with the FeH-H2 eutectic.
steps.quote: The melting point of non-magnetic FeH is higher than the eutectic melting temperature of FeHx (1 < x < 2)

steps.action: Set the spin-loss stabilization effect against other iron compounds (FeO, FeS, FeSi, Fe7C3, Fe7N3) and argued that the Fe7N3 melting curve could be redrawn.
steps.quote: The similar effect has not been reported for other iron compounds

steps.action: Rejected continuous Fe-FeH solid solution above about 40 GPa. Congruent melting at a temperature maximum, together with the hcp versus fcc structural difference, indicates a Fe-FeH eutectic system.
steps.quote: indicate that the Fe-FeH becomes a eutectic system above ∼40 GPa

steps.action: Extrapolated the fitted model to inner-core pressures and computed the Fe phase diagram. FeH melts at 5500 K at 330 GPa.
steps.quote: It shows that the melting point of stoichiometric FeH is 5500 K at 330 GPa

steps.action: Compared the FeH melting curve with published curves for FeSi, FeO, FeS and Fe3C and with the modelled Fe curve. The FeH dT/dP slope is similar to that of Fe, and FeH melts about 350 K lower at the CMB and ICB.
steps.quote: On the other hand, it is similar to that of pure Fe

steps.action: Kept the Fe-FeH eutectic with a nearly pressure-independent eutectic liquid composition, taking FeH0.42 at about 40 GPa from Oka et al. (2022). This gives an upper bound of 0.75 wt% H in the outer core.
steps.quote: The eutectic liquid composition of FeH0.42 estimated at ∼40 GPa may also change little with increasing pressure.

tree.answer: Melting behaviour of non-magnetic fcc FeH and Fe-FeH phase relations at core pressures, previously unknown
No; melting is inferred from hazy XRD signals on quench, cross-checked by melting texture
Determine the FeH melting curve 43-152 GPa and the form of the Fe-FeH diagram
Continuous solid solution (Fukai 1992) versus eutectic system due to the structural and magnetic change
Under the eutectic rival, FeH melts congruently at a temperature maximum above the FeHx eutectic; under solid solution, the FeH solidus equals the FeH-H2 eutectic
Set: laser-heated DAC with H-undersaturated stoichiometric FeH
Melting criterion cross-checked by SEM texture; stoichiometry controls; no parameter sensitivity tests of the model
Melting curve estimated; Fe-FeH eutectic above about 40 GPa kept; solid solution rejected at high pressure

end.claim: Non-magnetic stoichiometric FeH melts congruently along a steep melting curve, bracketed from 43 to 152 GPa (about 2100-4600 K, ±5% in temperature) and similar in slope to Fe, which implies an Fe-FeH eutectic above about 40 GPa.

decisive_move.sentence: The in situ XRD detection of hazy quench signals bracketing melting in each run, without which neither the melting curve nor congruent melting would be established.

gates.evidence: The structural and magnetic expectation from Tagawa et al. (2022) directed the choice to measure melting of non-magnetic FeH, and runs #4-#5 were placed near the spin-loss pressure (p. 6). The melting brackets could have failed: the hazy-signal criterion was cross-checked by SEM texture (p. 6). The eutectic claim follows from congruent melting plus the structural argument rather than from a direct test. Nothing was stated as fixed in advance.

imports.item: CALPHAD-type free-energy models for Fe-Sm and Fe-Ti hydrides (Kivilahti & Miettinen 1987; Zinkevich et al. 2002)
Nonlinear minimization in R (R Core Team 2018)
Synchrotron X-ray diffraction at SPring-8 BL10XU
Focused ion beam milling and field-emission SEM
Quench microstructure as a melting signature (Hrubiak et al. 2017, molybdenum)

novelty_claims.quote: The melting curve of non-magnetic fcc FeH is not known.
The similar effect has not been reported for other iron compounds because it has not been explored nor carefully examined.

limits: No review file was supplied, so no review sequence is coded; the acknowledgments mention two referees (p. 10). Sub-claims sit at different statuses: congruent melting rests on the absence of other quench phases; the Fe-FeH eutectic above about 40 GPa is best_explanation, inferred from congruent melting plus structural difference without measuring Fe-rich compositions; the pressure-independent eutectic composition FeH0.42 and the 0.75 wt% H upper bound are a weaker inference, built on the Oka et al. (2022) preprint from the same group and on similar dT/dP slopes. The extrapolation to 330 GPa is untested. Model sensitivity is not explored: the trade-off between magnetic moment and liquid bulk modulus is acknowledged but not quantified (p. 7). Temperature uncertainty (±5%) and the NaCl pressure validation are imported from earlier work. Composition is none_fits: the walk is a laboratory property measurement under set conditions followed by model fitting and an indirect rival exclusion, which matches neither strong_inference (no crucial test shared by rivals) nor trace_series. That classification is an inference.

disagreements.target: Fukai (1992) continuous Fe-FeH solid solution phase diagram
disagreements.support: The diagram is accepted below about 20 GPa but replaced by a eutectic above about 40 GPa, on the basis of congruent FeH melting and the hcp/fcc structural difference.
disagreements.quote: indicate that the Fe-FeH becomes a eutectic system above ∼40 GPa

disagreements.target: Kusakabe et al. (2019) Fe7N3 melting curve
disagreements.support: The authors argue by analogy with Fe7C3 spin loss above 53 GPa that the curve neglects the magnetic transition and could be redrawn with a steeper slope.
disagreements.quote: The melting curve of Fe7N3 was determined without considering the effect of the magnetic transition (Kusakabe et al., 2019)

disagreements.support: The authors argue that DAC-only measurements make a 7 GPa spin-transition anomaly difficult to observe.
disagreements.quote: with which anomalies at 7 GPa are difficult to observe

disagreements.target: Umemoto & Hirose (2015, 2020): up to 1.0 wt% H in the outer core
disagreements.support: The eutectic composition sets a lower maximum hydrogen content, or else FeH would crystallize at the ICB.
disagreements.quote: FeH0.42 (Fe + 0.75 wt% H) could be the maximum hydrogen concentration in the liquid core

alternatives_considered.chosen: Tmax (peak hot-spot temperature) as the melting temperature
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Tmean averaged over the 6 μm X-ray spot
alternatives_considered.reason: Tmax is more relevant to melting

alternatives_considered.chosen: NaCl pressure medium as the pressure marker at high temperature
alternatives_considered.reason: Validated in Tagawa et al. (2022), where NaCl gave pressures very similar to KCl

alternatives_considered.chosen: Endmember stoichiometric FeH with liquid properties specialized to x = 1
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Nonideal mixing terms across FeHx compositions
alternatives_considered.reason: Only the FeH composition is of interest, and the experiments give iso-composition melting points

alternatives_considered.chosen: No volume change modelled at the magnetic to non-magnetic transition
alternatives_considered.reason: Not clearly observed in the FeH compression curve; simplifies the model at the cost of poorer constraints on magnetic properties and liquid bulk modulus

alternatives_considered.chosen: FeS and Fe3C melting curves for comparison
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Fe2S and Fe7C3, the phases forming eutectics with Fe at ICB pressure
